verses.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Go in to Pharaoh, for I have hardened his heart, and the heart of his servants, that I may show these my signs among them,
and that you may tell in the hearing of your son, and of your son’s son, what things I have done to Egypt, and my signs which I have done among them; that you may know that I am Yahweh.”

Moses and Aaron went in to Pharaoh, and said to him, “This is what Yahweh, the God of the Hebrews, says: ‘How long will you refuse to humble yourself before me? Let my people go, that they may serve me.
Or else, if you refuse to let my people go, behold, tomorrow I will bring locusts into your country,

and they shall cover the surface of the earth, so that one won’t be able to see the earth. They shall eat the residue of that which has escaped, which remains to you from the hail, and shall eat every tree which grows for you out of the field.

Your houses shall be filled, and the houses of all your servants, and the houses of all the Egyptians; as neither your fathers nor your fathers’ fathers have seen, since the day that they were on the earth to this day.’” He turned, and went out from Pharaoh.
Pharaoh’s servants said to him, “How long will this man be a snare to us? Let the men go, that they may serve Yahweh, their God. Don’t you yet know that Egypt is destroyed?”
Moses and Aaron were brought again to Pharaoh, and he said to them, “Go, serve Yahweh your God; but who are those who will go?”
Moses said, “We will go with our young and with our old; with our sons and with our daughters, with our flocks and with our herds will we go; for we must hold a feast to Yahweh.”
He said to them, “Yahweh be with you if I will let you go with your little ones! See, evil is clearly before your faces.
Not so! Go now you who are men, and serve Yahweh; for that is what you desire!” They were driven out from Pharaoh’s presence.
Yahweh said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand over the land of Egypt for the locusts, that they may come up on the land of Egypt, and eat every herb of the land, even all that the hail has left.”
Moses stretched out his rod over the land of Egypt, and Yahweh brought an east wind on the land all that day, and all night; and when it was morning, the east wind brought the locusts.
The locusts went up over all the land of Egypt, and rested in all the borders of Egypt. They were very grievous. Before them there were no such locusts as they, nor will there ever be again.

For they covered the surface of the whole earth, so that the land was darkened, and they ate every herb of the land, and all the fruit of the trees which the hail had left. There remained nothing green, either tree or herb of the field, through all the land of Egypt.
Then Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron in haste, and he said, “I have sinned against Yahweh your God, and against you.
Now therefore please forgive my sin again, and pray to Yahweh your God, that he may also take away from me this death.”
He went out from Pharaoh, and prayed to Yahweh.
Yahweh turned an exceeding strong west wind, which took up the locusts, and drove them into the Red Sea.  There remained not one locust in all the borders of Egypt.
But Yahweh hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he didn’t let the children of Israel go.
Yahweh said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand toward the sky, that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt, even darkness which may be felt.”
Moses stretched out his hand toward the sky, and there was a thick darkness in all the land of Egypt for three days.
They didn’t see one another, and nobody rose from his place for three days; but all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings.
Pharaoh called to Moses, and said, “Go, serve Yahweh. Only let your flocks and your herds stay behind. Let your little ones also go with you.”
Moses said, “You must also give into our hand sacrifices and burnt offerings, that we may sacrifice to Yahweh our God.
Our livestock also shall go with us. Not a hoof shall be left behind, for of it we must take to serve Yahweh our God; and we don’t know with what we must serve Yahweh, until we come there.”
But Yahweh hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he wouldn’t let them go.
Pharaoh said to him, “Get away from me! Be careful to see my face no more; for in the day you see my face you shall die!”
Moses said, “You have spoken well. I will see your face again no more.”

footnotes.content: The Lord makes His purposes plain to Moses: hardness of heart is not beyond God's reach—it becomes the very stage for His signs. I'm struck by how candid He is about what He will do and why. This is a God who does not hide His works but declares them openly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here the Lord looks forward to a grandmother's knee, a grandfather's memory. What He does in Egypt will be told again and again so that those yet unborn may know He is Yahweh. Every act of deliverance echoes into the future.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses and Aaron's question cuts to the heart: *How long will you refuse to humble yourself?* It's the simplest path laid before Pharaoh—humility—and yet it remains closed. The God of the Hebrews asks not for much, but for one thing: a bowed knee.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tomorrow the locusts come. There is still a choice, still a dawn, still time to turn. But Moses speaks of what *will* be, not what *might* be, because he knows the stubbornness that hardens the human heart when God offers grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The plague is described not with rage but almost with sorrow—covering the earth so completely that nothing green remains. It's the depth of want that follows upon the refusal of mercy. When a man will not bow, creation itself bows under judgment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Every house, from palace to servant's quarter, will be filled with locusts—a plague so complete that it exceeds what any grandfather's story could contain. The Lord levels the field of suffering. No one escapes but those who trust Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At last the servants speak what should have been spoken long ago: *Egypt is destroyed.* Their voice reaches Pharaoh's ear, but not his heart. Often the wise words of those around us cannot move us if pride has built a wall.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh offers a half-permission—go, serve your God, but who exactly? The question itself is an attempt at control, a bargaining when there is nothing left to bargain with. The hardened heart seeks compromise where only surrender will do.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses names it clearly: all must go—young and old, sons and daughters, flocks and herds—*for we must hold a feast to Yahweh.* There is no such thing as worship with half your heart or half your house. When we gather before the Lord, we bring all of ourselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh sees what he fears—children, the vulnerable, the future—and calls it *evil.* His refusal now shows its true face: not economy or statecraft, but the hardness that calls protection of the weak a curse and a threat.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king makes a final counteroffer: men may go, but not the children. And with that division rejected, all are driven out. Sometimes the Lord's yes cannot be split into pieces, and when we try, His hand closes the door.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord speaks to Moses with absolute simplicity: stretch out your hand. The rod is not magic; it is obedience made visible. Even at the edge of the sea, the greatest acts of God rest on a human hand willing to rise and move.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The east wind—the desert wind that brings not life but devastation. In the language of Egypt itself, the wind speaks judgment. And in the morning the locusts arrive, as if the very sky itself obeys the God of the Hebrews.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The text breaks its own measure to say it plainly: *never such locusts, nor will there ever be again.* History itself closes behind this plague. Some judgments stand alone because the stubbornness that called them forth may never be matched.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Darkness visible—the land blackened by locusts, every green thing consumed, nothing left but want. It's a portrait of what it means to refuse the Lord's hand: the world itself becomes poor, emptied, without hope of spring.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now Pharaoh calls in haste—crisis has eroded the walls of pride at last. His words come quickly: *I have sinned against Yahweh your God, and against you.* Confession is simple when the alternative is to watch your kingdom consumed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He asks forgiveness *again*—as if forgiveness grows tired. And he begs Moses to pray: *take away this death.* His own words reveal the confusion of a hardened heart—he can feel the weight of judgment but cannot see the mercy that moves beneath it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses went out and prayed. In a single sentence lies the work of intercession—the obedience of the one who speaks for the people. Prayer is sometimes the simplest thing a faithful servant can do.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The west wind—the sea wind that returns as swiftly as it came—sweeps the locusts into the Red Sea. Not one remains. The Lord shows Pharaoh, once more, that creation itself obeys His word, that even the wind bends to His purpose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yet Yahweh hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he would not let them go. The cycle turns again. Mercy arrived, was rejected, turned back to stone. This is the terrible freedom of the human will—to say no even when the answer costs everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now the Lord moves to darkness itself—not the dark of evening but a darkness *that may be felt.* It is not mere absence but presence of blindness, a weight upon the eyes and heart of a nation that would not see.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three days of thick darkness. For seventy-two hours, Egypt sits in blindness—no work, no movement, no comfort of light. It is a foretaste of what the soul knows when it turns from God: the world goes dark and thin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They could not see one another, and no one rose from his place—Egypt paralyzed in shadow. But the children of Israel had light in their dwellings. Even here, division is drawn: darkness for those who refuse, light for those who trust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Again Pharaoh calls Moses—now he says they may go, even the little ones may go, but the flocks and herds must stay. One final attempt to keep something back, to retain a claim on Israel's future. But the Lord does not negotiate in pieces.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses answers with patient firmness: we must also have sacrifices and burnt offerings for the Lord. Nothing is to be left behind because nothing that belongs to the Lord can be held back by human hands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Not a hoof shall be left behind—because when we worship, we offer *all* we have. Moses names this plainly: we don't yet know what the Lord will ask of us until we arrive at the place. True worship comes with empty hands and a full heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But Yahweh hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he would not let them go. The refusal becomes absolute now, hardened past any give, past any moment of return. Some doors, once closed by pride, stay closed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Get away from me—Pharaoh's voice drops to a whisper of final rejection. He sets an ultimatum: see my face again and die. It's the threat of a king with nowhere left to stand, clinging to authority as it crumbles.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You have spoken well—Moses accepts the hard boundary with a quiet grace. Readers today hear an echo of how the righteous often see more clearly than kings: that some roads end, some doors close, and the faithful know when to step back and let the Lord's hand fall.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
